title: Profitability Decline: Diagnose Why Profits Are Falling
prompt: Our client is a regional coffee-shop chain with about 200 stores. Over the last two years their total profit has fallen roughly 20% even though revenue is flat. The CEO wants to understand why and what to do. How would you approach this?
blurb: A profit-decline diagnosis — break profit into a clean revenue/cost tree, isolate the driver, and recommend a fix.

rubric.label: Profit-tree structure
rubric.description: Decomposes profit = revenue - cost and breaks each side down cleanly (revenue = # customers x avg ticket, or price x volume; cost = fixed vs variable, by line item) in a MECE way before diving in.

rubric.label: Hypothesis-driven isolation
rubric.description: Uses the 'revenue flat but profit down' clue to hypothesize the problem is on the cost side (or a revenue mix shift), and drives the diagnosis to isolate the specific driver rather than exploring randomly.

rubric.label: Quantitative rigor
rubric.description: Reads the numbers given, does the arithmetic to quantify each driver's contribution to the 20% decline, and identifies the biggest lever — carries units and percentages.

rubric.label: Business judgment
rubric.description: Interprets the root cause in business terms (e.g. commodity input inflation, wage pressure, a per-store fixed-cost problem) and proposes actionable, prioritized fixes with tradeoffs.

rubric.label: Synthesis & recommendation
rubric.description: Summarizes the diagnosis and a prioritized recommendation clearly, tying the fix back to the CEO's question.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Signposts each branch of the tree, states what they'd check and why, and adapts as data arrives.

reference.scenario: Client: 200-store regional coffee chain. Revenue flat ~$200M/yr over two years; profit down ~20% (from ~$24M to ~$19M, i.e. ~12% to ~9.5% margin). Interviewer facts to reveal on request: revenue is flat in dollars but transaction VOLUME is down ~8% while average ticket is UP ~9% (they raised prices to offset inflation); on the cost side, cost of goods (coffee beans, milk, cups) rose ~15% driven by a coffee-bean commodity spike, and labor cost per store rose ~10% from wage increases; rent and other fixed costs are flat. Store count is unchanged. So: they held revenue by raising prices, but volume erosion plus input and wage inflation compressed margin. The bean spike is partly cyclical; wage increases are structural.
model_points: Restate and quantify the problem: profit down 20% on flat revenue means margin compressed — the issue is a widening gap between revenue and cost, so anchor on the cost side and on mix, not top-line growth.

Build a profit tree: Profit = Revenue - Cost. Revenue = # transactions x average ticket. Cost = COGS (variable: beans, milk, cups) + Labor + Fixed (rent, utilities, overhead). Optionally per-store to normalize.
Decompose revenue: flat dollars hides that volume is down ~8% while ticket is up ~9% — a price-for-volume trade that signals demand softness and a possible longer-term revenue risk.
Decompose cost: quantify which lines moved — COGS up ~15% (bean commodity spike), labor up ~10% (wages); rent flat. Attribute the margin loss to these.
Isolate the biggest driver with arithmetic: on ~$200M revenue, a COGS increase and a labor increase each shave points off margin; identify which contributes more to the ~$5M profit drop.
Interpret: distinguish cyclical (bean price) from structural (wages, volume erosion) causes — the fixes differ.

Recommend, prioritized: hedge/renegotiate bean supply and adjust menu/portion for input cost; address labor productivity (scheduling, throughput) rather than blunt wage cuts; and investigate the 8% volume decline before further price hikes erode traffic.
Synthesize: the CEO's profit fell because input and wage inflation outran the price increases, and price hikes are now costing volume — recommend supply-cost action plus a traffic/retention play.

probes.trigger: candidate starts listing costs without a tree
probes.question: Before we dig in, give me the structure — how does profit break down, and given the clue that revenue is flat but profit is down, where would you look first?
Revenue is flat in dollars — but transaction volume is down about 8% while average ticket is up about 9%. What does that tell you, and does it change where the problem is?
Cost of goods rose about 15% and labor per store about 10%; rent is flat. Which of these is doing more damage to profit — show me the math.

probes.trigger: candidate quantifies one driver but not both
probes.question: Roughly how much of the ~$5M profit decline comes from COGS versus labor? Which do you attack first?

probes.trigger: candidate blames only the bean price
probes.question: The bean spike may be cyclical. Which of these cost pressures is structural, and how does that change your recommendation?
You've raised prices and lost 8% of traffic. What would you do about volume before pushing price further?

red_flags: No structure — dives into random cost items without a profit tree
Misses the key clue: treats flat revenue as 'revenue is fine' and never inspects volume vs price mix
No quantification of how much each driver contributes to the decline
Confuses cyclical and structural causes, or proposes only one-off fixes
Recommends blunt cost-cutting (fire staff, slash quality) without considering volume or brand impact
No prioritized recommendation tied to the CEO's question
follow_ups: If the bean price is expected to normalize next year, would you still change the menu or supply strategy? Why?
Volume is down 8% — how would you figure out whether that's your price increase, a new competitor, or a demand shift?
The CEO wants profit back to 12% margin in a year. Is that realistic, and what levers get you there fastest?
How would per-store variance change your approach — what if 20 stores account for most of the decline?
reference.exemplar_answer: A strong candidate restates the problem quantitatively — 20% profit drop on flat revenue is a margin story, so the answer lives on the cost side or in revenue mix — then builds a clean profit tree (Profit = Revenue - Cost; Revenue = transactions x ticket; Cost = COGS + labor + fixed). Investigating revenue, they surface that flat dollars mask an ~8% volume decline offset by a ~9% price increase, flagging both a demand-softness risk and that further price hikes are dangerous. On cost, they quantify COGS up ~15% (a cyclical bean spike) and labor up ~10% (structural wage pressure), attribute the bulk of the ~$5M decline to these, and note fixed costs are flat. They separate cyclical from structural causes and recommend, in priority order: hedge/renegotiate bean supply and tune portions to blunt COGS; lift labor productivity via scheduling and throughput rather than headcount cuts; and diagnose the 8% traffic loss before raising price again. They close top-down: 'Margin fell because input and wage inflation outran your price increases, and the price increases are now costing you traffic — fix the supply cost, protect volume, and don't rely on price alone.'

interviewer_notes: This is a bread-and-butter profitability case; the mid-level bar is a clean profit tree plus disciplined use of the 'flat revenue, falling profit' clue. Do not volunteer numbers — reward the candidate for asking for revenue decomposition and cost line items. When they ask about revenue, drop the volume-down/ticket-up split and see if they catch the demand-erosion implication. Make them do the arithmetic attributing the ~$5M drop to COGS vs labor. Watch for the cyclical-vs-structural distinction — that separates a strong mid from an average one. Save the last two minutes for a prioritized recommendation and one follow-up on the volume decline.
